At midnight, I found a door between a locksmith and a bakery, though I had walked that street for years without noticing it. The sign above the frame read: Museum of Things Not Yet Found. A brass plaque below it seemed newly installed, its surface blank except for a tiny painted moon. I had been carrying a paper bag of oranges, a letter I did not plan to send, and the peculiar certainty that I was tired of explaining myself. The door opened before I touched it. Inside, a bell rang somewhere along a corridor lit by bright blue lanterns.

A woman in a gray coat sat behind a curved desk, sorting cards into piles that seemed to multiply whenever she looked away. She asked for my admission ticket. I had no ticket, but the oranges began glowing faintly, and the letter in my pocket grew warm. Perhaps it contained an invitation written by someone I had not yet become. The woman studied the bag, then the letter, then me. She said admission was free for those carrying something they intended to forget. I had forgotten. She slid me a card. It was mine, though I could not read it.

Beyond the desk stretched a corridor lined with doors, each bearing a small brass label. The first read: Things You Almost Said. Behind its frosted glass I heard voices arguing in gentle, familiar tones. The second door said: Maps of Places Never Visited. A boy peeked through it, wearing my posture and an expression I recognized from school photographs. The third door had no label at all, only a keyhole shaped like an ear. From beyond it came the sound of rain, bicycle bells, and my grandmother humming while cooking. I put my hand against the wood. It felt warm.

The gray-coated woman appeared behind me without footsteps. She pointed to the keyhole and said the lock changed shape for every visitor. I reached into my paper bag and found a key I did not remember pocketing. It was small, silver, and cool as a winter window. The woman smiled as though I had passed some invisible test. I inserted the key, turned it, and heard a soft click like an eye opening. The door exhaled a breath of lavender and dust, revealing a round room filled with stars. Not paper stars, not glass ones, but actual stars suspended overhead.

I entered slowly, carrying the oranges like offerings. The woman remained in the doorway, though her reflection wandered among the constellations. Each star cast a tiny shadow on the wooden floor, and the shadows moved whenever their stars thought no one was watching. Near the center stood a brass telescope pointed not upward but into my chest. A card appeared on its base. This time I could read it: For Every Distance There Is Another Way Home. The words rearranged themselves into an address I knew but could never have written. Below, a date shone like a small white star.

I asked the woman what day the date represented. She said dates in this room were less questions than doors. I looked through the telescope and saw a kitchen I had left thirty years ago, its blue cupboards glowing under morning light. My younger self sat at the table, turning a smooth stone between her fingers. She looked up at me with the stern suspicion reserved for strangers and the kind things we trust with our memories. She placed the stone in my palm, then shook her head. Some lessons arrive only when we stop demanding that they arrive sooner.

I placed the stone in my pocket, where it immediately became heavier than the oranges. The kitchen vanished, but the taste of bitter coffee remained. The woman led me past the star room into a gallery of ordinary miracles: a match striking itself on the first try, two strangers remembering each other’s names, rain landing only on the rooftops of houses where someone was waiting. There were darker exhibits: an apology delivered perfectly, too late; a door opened just after someone needed it; a map drawn by every traveler except the one who stayed. I recognized too many of them.

“Why did you stay?” the woman asked. I had not noticed her following us into the gallery. “Because I was afraid that moving would make me forget,” I said. “Or perhaps because I was afraid that remembering would make moving impossible.” She nodded as if this were the correct answer. Behind us, the darker exhibits folded into a single door. Its label read: Reasons We Did Not Go. I pushed it open. Beyond waited a wide field under a green sky, full of people walking in every direction yet leaving no footprints. In their hands they carried empty glass jars.

The woman handed me a jar. Inside, a patch of blue drifted like smoke, carrying a pale sun, several birds, and the distant roof of a house I had been trying to remember. I shook it gently, and the contents expanded until the woman stood beside me beneath a second sun. She looked tired suddenly, as though carrying daylight made hearts heavier. We walked together through the field. The people around us moved in silence, each gathering skies they had outgrown. Some held storms, others the first frost of winter. One child caught a golden hour, laughed, and released it.

The sky softened into pearl as the museum began closing itself with the patience of a book. I returned the jar to the woman. Her coat had turned white, and the desk had become a bench. She said everyone received one thing: a map, a memory, or a question. I had received all three. Outside, the baker shaped his first loaves, and the locksmith tested keys against locks whose doors had not been built. The letter in my coat bore an address. I knew the street, though not the house. At the corner, a blue door waited beneath a moon.
